Abstract
Diagnosing a whole-slide image is an interactive, multistage process, yet
practical agentic systems that navigate fields, adjust magnification and
deliver explainable diagnoses remain lacking, largely because the tacit,
experience-based viewing behaviour of expert pathologists is absent
from model training data. Here we introduce Pathology-CoT, a
framework that converts expert viewing chain-of-thought behaviour into
scalable agent supervision through three contributions. First, an artificial
intelligence session recorder unobtrusively captures routine navigation in
standard whole-slide image viewers and converts raw logs into
standardized behavioural commands and bounding boxes. Second, a
human-in-the-loop review pipeline turns artificial intelligence-drafted
rationales into paired ‘where to look’ and ‘why it matters’ supervision,
enabling sixfold faster labelling. Third, using these data, we built
Pathology-o3, a two-stage agent that proposes regions of interest and
performs behaviour-guided reasoning. On gastrointestinal lymph node
metastasis detection, Pathology-o3 outperformed state-of-the-art vision–
language models, showed consistent gains across multiple vision–
language model backbones and maintained strong performance on an
independent external validation cohort.

Data availability
The Pathology-CoT Chain-of-Thought dataset for the skin cancer cohort,
together with the trained behaviour predictors for both the Stanford CRC
lymph node and skin cancer cohorts, is publicly available via GitHub at
https://github.com/zhihuanglab/Pathology-CoT. WSIs and expert
annotations from the LNCO2 dataset are available via the AIDA Data
Hub at https://datahub.aida.scilifelab.se/10.23698/aida/lnco2 upon
application and approval. WSIs and expert annotations from the DROID
skin dataset are available via the AIDA Data Hub at https://
datahub.aida.scilifelab.se/10.23698/aida/drsk upon application and
approval. Source data are provided with this paper.
Code availability
Source code is publicly available via GitHub at https://github.com/
zhihuanglab/Pathology-CoT.

Extended data
Extended Data Fig. 1 The Behaviour Analysis Pipeline for
Preprocessing Pathologist Navigation.
The process transforms raw, high-frequency viewport data into a clean
set of actions. From left to right: (1) Raw Behaviour: The initial noisy

data with many overlapping viewports. (2) Initial Action Segmentation:
Raw events are grouped into StayInspect (blue) and PanInspect (red)
actions based on temporal heuristics. (3) Filtering Overview Actions:
Very large, low-magnification bounding boxes corresponding to non-
diagnostic overviews are removed. (4) Merging Overlapping Actions:
Spatially-proximal actions with high IoU are merged into single,
consolidated actions. (5) Pruning Containing Actions: Larger,
redundant actions that fully contain smaller, more specific inspection
actions are pruned. (6) Normalizing Action Bounding Boxes: The final
set of actions is resized to standard dimensions corresponding to
discrete magnification levels (for example, 5 × , 10 ×), creating a
consistent input format for the VLM.
Extended Data Fig. 2 Validation of AI Session Recorder
against biological eye-tracking data.
(Top Row) Visualization of raw behavioural signals from a first-year
resident (left, exhibiting exploratory navigation) and a senior attending
pathologist with 30 years of experience (right, exhibiting targeted
navigation). Red dots indicate ground-truth eye fixation points recorded
by an eye-tracker; yellow and blue outlines represent raw mouse and
viewport movements, respectively. (Bottom Row) The corresponding
discrete output generated by the AI Session Recorder.
Extended Data Fig. 3 Comparison of AI Session Recorder-
generated Inspect ROI results from two sessions from the
same attending pathologist.

The same pathologist generates very similar results across different
sessions, showing the stability and reliability of AI Session Recorder.
Extended Data Fig. 4 Performance stratification by tumor
burden on colorectal cancer lymph node metastasis.
a Stratified performance analysis on colorectal cancer lymph node
metastasis cases sorted by difficulty. Isolated Tumor Cells (ITCs, ≤0.2
mm, n=5), Micrometastasis (0.2–2 mm, n=13), and Macrometastasis (> 2
mm, n=29). We compare Pathology-o3 against the best proprietary
model (GPT-4.1), best open-source model (InternVL3), and a baseline
model (Llama-4). b Visualization of zoom-in behaviours on
Micrometastasis and ITCs across Claude, Gemini, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-
mini, Pathology-o3, and an attending pathologist. Pathology-o3
demonstrates navigation patterns highly aligned with the attending
pathologist, successfully locating tumor clusters that lack desmoplastic
reaction (typically absent in ITCs), whereas other models often fail to
focus on diagnostic regions.
Source data
Extended Data Fig. 5 Quantitative attribution of Behaviour
Predictor attention drivers.
a Illustration of the automated classification logic used to distinguish
“Structure” from “Pathology” based on spatial intersection with ground
truth masks. Green contours delineate normal physiological structures
(for example, healthy dermis/epidermis), while red dotted contours mark

pathological regions (for example, tumor nests, inflammation). Predicted
ROIs are classified strictly based on their overlap: blue bounding boxes
indicate model attention on confirmed normal anatomy ("Structure”),
whereas red bounding boxes indicate attention on confirmed
abnormalities ("Pathology”). This protocol ensures objective
categorization of the model’s viewing behaviour. b Quantitative
attribution of model attention drivers using the DROID segmentation
ontology. Left: Distribution of the 960 highest-confidence ROIs predicted
by the YOLOv8-Large model. The majority of attention (62.9%) is
allocated to normal anatomical structures (for example, epidermis, skin
appendages) rather than explicit pathology, reflecting a screening-like
behaviour pattern. Right: Granular breakdown of the ROIs classified as
“Pathology” (N=340). Notably, the model identifies not only frank
neoplasms (BCC, Melanocytic Neoplasm, SCC) but also subtle non-
neoplastic findings (33.5%), which include inflammation, scarring, and
other cellular responses. “Non-informative” refers to background, ink, or
blur.
Source data
Extended Data Fig. 6 Localization of suspicious regions
across different VLMs on DROID skin dataset.
Comparison of region-of-interest (ROI) identification among a Gemini-3-
Pro, b Gemini-2.5-Pro, c GPT-5.2, and d our specialized Pathology-o3.
Extended Data Fig. 7 Ablation study of Behaviour

Predictor scale on Dermatopathology ROI prediction.
We compared predictions from YOLOv8 architectures of increasing
capacity (Nano to Large) on the same slides. The comparison illustrates
that while smaller models (Nano/Small) are easily misled by local
artifacts (for example, incorrectly identifying ink or blood as ROIs,
marked with green question marks), larger models (Medium/Large)
demonstrate a superior understanding of global tissue structure, correctly
focusing on anatomical context while ignoring distractors.
